This series asks how far public medicine data can ease the problems pharmacies face. The perspective is that of **those who could help pharmacies with ordering, stock and return information** (distributors, pharmacy support services). Each page starts from what makes pharmacy work hard and ends with what public information can tell in advance. The full Korean version of this overview is [here](../../../ko/posts/2026-11-pharm-data-series/index.qmd).

| Pain point | Question | Page |
|---|---|---|
| **Holding stock:** stock loses value when prices are cut | How many days ahead can a pharmacy know about a cut, how small is it, and can announced cuts be trusted? | [Only in 2024 could most price cuts be seen a month ahead](../2026-11-benefit-change-lead/index.qmd) |
| **Procuring:** drugs cannot be obtained on time | How well can ingredient-level prescriptions be forecast, and where do forecasts go most wrong? | [Prescription forecasts missed most for winter respiratory drugs and antibiotics](../2026-11-drug-demand-forecast/index.qmd) |
| **Procuring:** cold medicines and antibiotics run short every winter | Does any public signal announce winter prescription rises months ahead? | [No signal was found that announces winter prescription rises months ahead](../2026-11-winter-leading-signals/index.qmd) |
| (Verification) | How were those numbers checked? | [Demand forecasting technical note](../2026-11-drug-demand-tech-note/index.qmd) |

## Why these questions {#why}

| Stage | Question | What leaks | Felt rank | Public data coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Procuring | Can the drugs needed be obtained on time, in the amount needed? | Time, dispensing opportunities | 1 | **Partly.** Demand (prescriptions) and the number of substitutes; not shortages, allocation or stock |
| B. Holding stock | Does stock already bought keep its value? | Money | 2 (worsening fastest) | **Most.** What is cut, when and by how much |
| C. Dispensing | Is dispensing manageable? | Time, consumables, disputes | 3 | Weakly. Volume per prescription |
| D. Earning | Are sales and margins holding? | Sales | 4 | None. No pharmacy- or area-level data |

Procuring is felt most today; holding stock is a close second and is expected to worsen fastest as listed drugs are re-evaluated from 2027. The stages are linked: when drugs are hard to get, pharmacies stock up, and stock loses value when prices are cut.

**What public data can and cannot do.** They can tell in advance what will be cut, when and by how much; single out ingredients whose demand swings; and show how far announcements can be trusted. They cannot compute a pharmacy's losses (that needs its stock records), forecast shortages (no supply or stock data), or change compensation and return terms. The pain points and cases rest mainly on trade press and pharmacist surveys, which may lean towards reported harm.

## Does combining the two datasets help? {#list-price}

**Adding reimbursement-list price information to demand forecasts did not show an improvement.** With the price changes visible in the list at forecast time, unit-price forecast error was 0.0186 vs 0.0217, about 15% lower, but p = 0.252 could not be told apart from chance, nor from forecasts with the timing deliberately shifted. For prescription volume, the test could not even detect a deliberately injected 20% effect. The median pass-through from list price change to claimed unit price was only 0.55. The series therefore uses the reimbursement list for price and suspension alerts and the usage statistics for demand. The table is in the [technical note](../2026-11-drug-demand-tech-note/index.qmd#list-price-test).

## Ground rules

- A future date in the remarks is an **announcement**, not a change. Pages say "a cut was announced" or "realization rate 99.96%", never "the price was cut".
- Price changes and prescription volume are compared only as before-and-after changes and associations, not as causes.
- Demand forecasts are national and per ingredient, not order quantities for a pharmacy or product.
- No savings or incentive amounts are computed.
- The data contain no shortages, product-level sales, pharmacy purchases or stock, wholesale distribution, or planned delisting dates.

## Next analyses {#next}

The guiding rule is to start with **the analysis that meets the least resistance and is feasible within the constraints**. The order follows the pain points above, weighted by how much information can reduce them and by what is coming (re-evaluation of listed drugs from 2027). "Possible now" means the public data already in hand are enough.

| # | Analysis | Pain point | Why | Possible now? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **How far ahead can a cut be known:** split cuts into cuts announced in the remarks, government bulk cuts and other cuts; measure the share visible in the list at least a month ahead and the size of cuts (won and percent) | Stock value | Answers "we only learn days before, so we give up checking" and "1-won cuts are a loss we just absorb" with numbers | **Done (2026-11-27).** Seeing a cut a month ahead happened mostly in 2024 (80.8%; 0–0.35% in other years). Bulk cuts were known 4–13 days ahead through notices and association guidance; 19.6% of the 2026-01 actual-transaction-price cuts were 1 won. [2nd edition](../2026-11-benefit-change-lead/index.qmd#lead) |
| 2 | **Re-evaluation exposure map:** describe which products were cut in the 2023-09 base-requirement re-evaluation, and count products in today's list with similar characteristics | Stock value | The pain point expected to worsen fastest | Possible now (descriptive). There has been essentially one bulk re-evaluation, so no predictive model |
| 3 | **Supply-vulnerability map:** trend of listed products and companies per ingredient, delistings, suspensions and price-ceiling increases, to find ingredients with few substitutes | Procurement | The part of shortages that public data can address is "can it be substituted?" | Map possible now. Matching with actual shortages needs supply-interruption reports; until then results are "vulnerability candidates" |
| 4 | **Delisting, suspension and unsellable stock:** was there a signal before a product left the list or was suspended, and how many same-ingredient substitutes existed then | Stock value | Can warn about stock that may become unreturnable | Possible now. Planned delisting dates are not in the data |
| 5 | **Reported shortage cases:** did ingredient prescriptions change sharply around reported shortages | Procurement | Links field complaints to data | Conditional. Ingredients with two or fewer companies are suppressed in the usage statistics; used as validation cases for #3 |
| 6 | **Leading signals for winter respiratory and antibiotic demand:** do search indices, paediatric care flows and the calendar move ahead of prescription increases | Procurement | Fever-reducer and antibiotic shortages cluster in winter and overlap with the largest forecast errors | **Exploration done (2026-11-26).** No signal 1–6 months ahead held up; current-month search acceleration moved with current-month prescription growth (a nowcast). [Results](../2026-11-winter-leading-signals/index.qmd). A province × month follow-up is being designed |
| 7 | **Long-term prescribing trend:** volume per claim by province, care-institution type and age | Dispensing | Long prescriptions add to stock and consumable burden | Possible but the indicator is weak: volume is in product units, not days supplied |

Warehouse-style pharmacies and dispensing fees per pharmacy are not covered: there are no pharmacy- or area-level data.

**Other candidates:** ingredient unit price around changes in the generic-substitution list, ingredient markets around patent expiry and generic entry, prescription flows by province and facility type, how combining strengths and forms affects forecast error, and an example of a single pharmacy alert built from the change log.
